# Verification planning and evidence

The goal is continuous production readiness: demonstrate the requested behavior and the affected
existing behavior, with honest evidence, while avoiding repeated work that cannot change the
answer. This rule resolves verification order and reuse in CPR current §E and §F. It does not
waive a failed requirement, invent a release approval, or turn a checklist into a build gate.

## Plan once, refresh on relevant change

Read the active scope, current handoff, applicable rules and last verification record once. Identify
the actual comparison base from the task, branch or pull request; do not assume `main`. Identify
the candidate including staged, unstaged and relevant untracked inputs. A commit name alone cannot
identify a dirty tree. Keep historical standards for provenance; read their unresolved applicable
sections on demand, not as a second competing workflow at every checkpoint.

Select checks by the behavior, shared dependencies and failure cases this change can affect. Name
the reason for each selection, the prerequisites, and any unverified area. A prerequisite is a real
data or artifact dependency, not a reason to stop unrelated checks. When impact is uncertain, shared
infrastructure changes broadly, or the final integration has no valid evidence, run the full
applicable required set. Final integration must have valid evidence for every applicable required
check; this can combine fresh execution and justified reuse, never an unexplained omission.

## Default order

1. During implementation, run focused tests and inexpensive checks; inspect newly introduced
   credentials early so they do not enter logs or commits. Demonstrate regression tests fail on the
   pre-fix behavior and pass on the fix.
2. At a coherent candidate, run the affected broader checks. Independent lint, type and test work
   can overlap within the shared resource budget. Review can inspect the stable candidate while
   checks run; its conclusion incorporates the completed results.
3. Build before checks that consume the built artifact. Browser and visual checks exercise that
   candidate, including affected neighboring surfaces. A source-server test is labeled as such;
   it does not establish that the release artifact works.
4. After review repairs, rerun affected checks and re-review the material fixes in a separate
   context. Reuse other valid evidence. If a check's inputs must change while it runs, stop it or
   run it against an immutable snapshot; never label a mixed-state result as a candidate pass.
5. Finish outgoing records, scan outgoing content and commits, and package final content once
   after review converges. Verify artifact identity and perform the environment-specific release
   checks. Generated output is scanned too when it is part of what will be delivered. A repair to
   an unrelated build does not invalidate a secret scan unless its scanned inputs change.

Dependency audits may run independently but use fresh advisory data. Do not serialize all work
behind an audit or secret scan merely because those checks appear late in a checklist.

## Evidence validity and reuse

Record the check id, exact command/options, original run id and execution time, result including
skips, input identity, tool and dependency versions, relevant configuration/environment identity,
and artifact or comparison-base identity when relevant. Do not record secrets in this metadata.
Use an opaque environment revision or a trusted local fingerprint for secret-bearing inputs.

The input set includes transitive dependencies, test files, fixtures, generated inputs, lockfiles,
build tools and relevant configuration, not just the directly changed source file. If a complete
set cannot be established, fingerprint the complete relevant tree or rerun. A changed commit SHA
alone does not invalidate identical inputs; a changed compiler or lockfile can invalidate them even
when source text is unchanged. Build/e2e evidence also covers the tested output and dependencies
of that output. A secret scan covers its base, outgoing commit set and final outgoing content.

Distinguish execution from applicability:

- **executed** — ran against the recorded inputs; retain the actual result.
- **reused — inputs unchanged** — a successful prior execution whose complete relevant inputs,
  environment and freshness conditions still match. Show the original time and run; it did not
  execute again. This is valid evidence for those inputs.
- **historical — invalidated or unproven** — useful provenance, not evidence of current acceptance.
- **not run / missing / blocked prerequisite** — say which and why; none is a pass.
- **not applicable** — record the applicability reason, not a fabricated execution result.

Only successful, complete deterministic results are candidates for automatic reuse. Do not reuse
a failed, interrupted or missing run as success. Retries preserve every attempt. A passing suite
with skipped cases still leaves those cases unverified. Reuse is not available when input coverage
or environment identity is unknown. External advisory, provider-health and deployment checks need
an explicit freshness policy and usually fresh execution; production side effects and load tests
are never replayed or skipped by a generic cache. A cache is local evidence, not a trust boundary:
untrusted reports cannot certify a release. Prefer a cache miss to incomplete provenance.

## Scheduling and server capacity

Requiredness and scheduling are separate. `required` decides how a selected check's result affects
the aggregate outcome; it does not imply a prerequisite, priority, concurrency slot, or freshness.
An optional check is not silently discarded: declare whether it is selected and report its result
or why it was not selected. A failed prerequisite prevents its dependent check from claiming a
pass, while independent checks can finish.

All agents and worktrees on the same server share one resource budget. Use the host's check-runner
coordinator or a shared queue/lock for expensive builds, browser suites and database tests, with
bounded workers inside each job. Set the budget from available CPU, memory and IO after reserving
capacity for the running application; two per-agent limits are not one shared limit. Start
conservatively when capacity is unknown. Never change another session's limits or kill its process
to obtain a slot. Record queue wait separately from execution duration. Coordinate commands started
outside the runner too, or record that they are outside the coordinator's coverage.

An independent reviewer inspects assertions, changed behavior and evidence provenance. It reuses
the implementer's valid captured results by default, runs targeted reproductions or missing checks,
and asks for broader validation only when impact or evidence requires it. A second full suite
started solely because another agent is reviewing does not improve independence.

## Portable runner configuration

Use `node .mock2/bin/check.mjs --list` to inspect the installed configuration. Named check ids also
select their transitive `dependsOn` prerequisites. `--json` returns the structured report;
`--no-reuse` forces fresh execution for a comparison or a suspected cache problem.

The `.mock2/checks.json` object contains a `checks` array and an optional `scheduler` object:

| Setting | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `scheduler.maxParallel` | Maximum admitted checks within this invocation. Legacy configs default to one. |
| `scheduler.sharedSlots` | Shared capacity for `resource: "shared"` checks across cooperating sessions. |
| `scheduler.budgetDir` | Optional shared coordination directory; use the same absolute location and slot count across worktrees. |
| `scheduler.queueTimeoutMs` | Bounded wait for capacity; a timeout is not a pass. |
| `dependsOn: ["build"]` | Actual prerequisite ids. Use for a browser check that consumes the build output. |
| `schedule: "always"` | Selected by the ordinary invocation. `"manual"` requires explicit selection or a dependent check. |
| `resource: "shared"` | Uses a shared slot. `"none"` explicitly exempts an inexpensive check; do not use it for heavy jobs. |
| `stage` | Reporting label such as `checks`, `browser` or `delivery`; a label does not enforce ordering. |

New templates declare two local workers and two shared slots; this is a configurable starting
point, not proof that two heavy jobs fit every server. The default shared directory is per OS user
under the system temporary directory. Different OS users, machines, containers with separate temp
directories, and commands outside the runner are not automatically coordinated: supply an
appropriate shared service or budget directory when they share the same constrained server.
All participants using one directory must agree on `sharedSlots`. Resolve stale ownership from
observed process state, never by stealing a reservation merely because it is old.

Automatic reuse is opt-in per check, with `reuse.deterministic: true`, `reuse.outputFree: true`,
nonempty `reuse.inputs` and `reuse.tools` arrays, and an explicit `reuse.env` array (which may be
empty). Inputs name actual files/directories, not globs or the repository root; include every
relevant source, fixture, configuration, lockfile and transitive input. Tool entries are safe
identity commands, for example `node --version`, not build commands. Declare relevant environment
names; the runner also fingerprints the inherited environment without recording its values.
`reuse.external: true` additionally requires a positive `reuse.maxAgeMs`, but cannot make a
nondeterministic provider probe or side effect suitable for caching.

This runner does not restore output artifacts. Do not opt builds, artifact-producing tests or
checks depending on mutable service state into reuse. Their dependent checks need the actual
artifacts and current state. Dependencies without a reusable input identity prevent automatic
reuse of their consumers. The `secrets` check always executes when selected; the runner rejects
cache configuration for it. Use focused check selection during edits and final outgoing scanning
for delivery instead of treating every edit as a full delivery run.

Reports are `.mock2/evidence/<runId>.json`; cache entries are under `.mock2/cache/`. The report's
`execution` is `executed`, `reused` or `not-run`, separate from status. `originalRunId`,
`originalFinishedAt`, `fingerprint` and `invalidationReason` preserve provenance; `queueMs` is
separate from execution `ms`. Saved reports use `commandHash`/`commandRef` and fingerprints instead
of raw command, environment or output text. Retain the referenced configuration/input revision
and redacted decisive output when a reviewer needs to reconstruct or assess the exact command.

## One run record, several views

Use one per-run machine-readable record as the source of commands, input identities, timings,
results, skips, reuse decisions, queue wait and attempts. Check-runner reports and Relay events can
provide those facts. The Markdown ledger, handoff and change record retain their roles but link to
that source or generate their repeated fields from it. Preserve user-written decisions and review
reasoning; write each rationale once and reference it. Never derive tool calls, model identity,
task start time or deployment success from check timings when the producer did not observe them.
Local `.mock2/cache/` and `.mock2/evidence/` are ignored generated state. Keep a redacted copy of
required evidence in the project's durable artifact store when another surface needs it; do not
commit secrets or raw sensitive logs. When no generator is installed, link the report and summarize
the needed facts once rather than
inventing a command or maintaining duplicate transcripts. Preserve existing history.

## Measuring a standards change

Separate **verification replay** from **whole-agent build performance**. Replay measures runner
overhead, order, caching and queueing on fixed inputs. It does not measure the time an agent takes
to understand, implement and repair a task.

For a before/after agent comparison, pin the same base commit, exact task and acceptance criteria,
model/version and reasoning settings, tools, dependency versions, server allocation and external
service fakes. Create isolated worktrees from that base; install the old standards in one and new
standards in the other. Start fresh agent contexts with equal supplied information. Never give one
arm the other's solution. Keep production data and deployment out of the experiment unless that
specific experiment is authorized.

Use several representative tasks and repeat paired trials because model output and host load
vary. Randomize or counterbalance old/new execution order. Run comparable trials without resource
contention, or keep and record the same controlled contention in both arms. Measure cold caches and
warm caches separately; never compare an old cold run with a new warm run. Reset or seed dependency,
build, check and application state consistently and name which caches are warm. Pin or record any
external data that cannot be made deterministic. Record failures and timeouts, not just successes.

An independent reviewer applies the same acceptance suite and review rubric to both outputs,
preferably without seeing the standards label. Include requested behavior, affected-neighbor
regressions, authorization/data boundaries, test quality and unresolved findings. Do not shorten
the acceptance suite to make the new workflow win. Also verify that the final artifact corresponds
to the tested candidate.

Report total wall time, active agent time when observed, check execution and queue time, repeated
checks and invalidation reasons, review/repair rounds, tool calls and token/cost figures when
available. Compare paired differences, median and range (or percentiles with sufficient trials),
alongside quality outcomes and uncertainty. One run is a smoke test, not a speed claim. Only call
the change faster at comparable quality; a cheaper run with missing acceptance evidence is not a
successful optimization. `CPR-v1.1-current.md` is accompanied by `Standards-Benchmark.md`, which
provides the repeatable replay command and the full-build experiment worksheet; replay results are
not a claim about whole-agent development speed.

# Comparing standards before and after

**Applies from Mock2 1.12.0.** Keep acceptance and safety requirements constant; measure whether a
new execution process reaches the same independently verified result with less elapsed time or
repeated work. Two complementary experiments answer different questions.

## 1. Reproducible check-runner comparison

The repository includes `scripts/benchmark-standards.mjs` and a deterministic validation fixture.
Run it from the Mock2 source repository with Node 18+ and Git, selecting the actual pre-change
revision. The candidate is the current runner file unless another file is supplied:

```sh
node scripts/benchmark-standards.mjs --baseline <pre-change-git-ref> --pairs 3 --output /tmp/mock2-runner-comparison.json
```

Alternatively, use `--baseline-file /path/to/old/check.mjs` and optionally
`--candidate-file /path/to/new/check.mjs`. The script refuses identical runner bundles and copies each version’s companion support file when present. Run only
trusted runner files: each runner is executable code. Every pair gets independent temporary Git
repositories and an isolated shared-worker budget, then runs the same commands in a seeded,
randomized baseline/candidate order. Temporary repositories are removed after the experiment.
The default seed is 137; choose another with `--seed <integer>` and record it.

The measured scenarios are:

| Scenario | Expected acceptance result | Evidence behavior under test |
|---|---|---|
| Cold | All three checks pass | No existing Mock2 evidence; all checks execute |
| Warm | All three checks pass | Unchanged deterministic inputs can reuse three results |
| Changed input, valid | All checks pass | Only the affected input invalidates its result |
| Changed input, invalid | The affected check fails | Stale success must not hide the injected defect |
| Same invalid input again | The same check fails | Failed evidence must not be reused as success |

The report includes actual subprocess wall time, runner duration when available, per-check
execution/reuse counts, queue times, hashes of both runners and the fixture, runtime version,
paired samples and median wall times. Its assertions use independently known fixture outcomes;
a faster run that misses the injected failure fails the experiment. No elapsed-time threshold is
enforced: a small workload can be slower when fingerprinting and coordination cost more than its
checks save. Report that result rather than suppressing it.

Here, **cold means an empty Mock2 evidence cache**, not an emptied operating-system cache or a
fresh dependency installation. The fixture does repeatable hashing and validates synthetic input;
it is neither an application build nor an AI-agent benchmark. Do not extrapolate its percentages
to VS Code development time. Recheck scheduling limits and warm evidence separately on the real
application's commands before drawing that conclusion.

## 2. Paired real-build experiment

Use an isolated, disposable copy of the actual application and a representative, bounded task,
such as adding one authorized admin filter with its expected neighboring-screen behavior. Keep
production data, recipients and deployments out of the experiment. Pin the starting repository
commit, task prompt, dependencies, Node/toolchain versions, environment fixtures, external stubs,
hardware and AI model/settings. Save exact copies or hashes of old and new standards. Provide the
same tools, access and acceptance requirements to both arms.

For each pair:

1. Create two independent worktrees or clean clones from the same starting commit. Install the old
   standards in one and the updated standards in the other; these are the experimental difference.
2. Start fresh agent sessions with the same task and initial context. Do not let the second session
   read the first result, transcript, cache, handoff or reasoning. Randomize which arm runs first.
3. Hold server capacity and background load comparable. On one server, run the arms sequentially;
   simultaneous runs compete for resources and contaminate timing. Apply the same shared resource
   ceiling. Warm dependency caches equally, or reset them equally and label the experiment cold.
4. Record wall time from task start to the first independently accepted candidate, active agent
   time, model/tool usage when exposed, review/fix cycles, executed and reused checks, queue time,
   test time, packaging time and infrastructure interruptions. Use timestamps rather than estimates.
5. Run a separate acceptance suite and review on each result. Keep acceptance tests outside the
   agent's editable worktree or validate their hashes. Include the requested behavior, affected
   neighbors, authorization, relevant security and negative cases. Reviewer evidence reuse must
   not replace this experiment's common acceptance oracle.
6. Count an incomplete, failing or regressed build as a failed trial, not as a fast completion.
   Report infrastructure failures separately with their reason; do not silently discard slow runs.

Use at least three paired runs, preferably five or more when costs permit, across a small UI task,
a behavior/API change and a migration or integration task if those represent the real workload.
Compare paired differences, median and range as well as acceptance/pass rate. Repeated runs
matter because agent decisions and external services vary even with pinned settings. Fix acceptance
criteria before collecting results; avoid selecting only tasks that favor the new process.

Use distinct cold and warm experiments. A warm run may reuse evidence from the *same arm's*
unchanged inputs; it must not inherit the other arm's completed solution. Include a controlled
source/configuration change and an injected failing case to verify that reuse expires correctly.
Record external checks with their freshness requirements; never reuse yesterday's provider health
as current health merely to improve timing.

A useful result reads: “Across five paired runs of task X, updated standards reached independent
acceptance in median Y minutes versus Z, with A/B accepted candidates, C fewer repeated checks and
D minutes of queue time.” Until this experiment runs, state that end-to-end build speed is unmeasured.

## Decision rule

Adopt an optimization when common acceptance stays satisfied and it meaningfully improves the
workload's time or consistency. Preserve required evidence, truthful status and failure detection.
If verification is already a small part of total time, inspect implementation, model latency,
review loops, context loading or server contention rather than removing useful tests.

# Stack versions and compatibility

`stack.versions.json` is the canonical release baseline. `Stack-Version-Table.md` is generated from
it. Every baseline is immutable within a published Mock2 release; a regular review produces a new
dated baseline. Review at least monthly and on an upstream security advisory or support change.
This is a review obligation, not a new release approval gate. Check official release metadata,
support status, engine/peer requirements and migration notes before changing a pin. Never resolve
`latest`, a floating image tag, or an old remembered default during an application build.

For **new CPR applications**, select `cpr-2026-10-03`: Node 24 LTS, PostgreSQL 18 and the exact
selected packages in the registry. The selected package combination has a reproducible compatibility
fixture; its evidence names the actual runtime, commands and scope. Package compatibility does not
prove a particular application's authorization, migrations, browser behavior, object provider or
production performance. Validate those affected contracts during implementation. Optional tools
are selected only when used; a pin is not permission to add a capability outside the task.

For **existing applications**, capture their actual stack in project-owned `state/stack.json` and
retain its major/minor lines. Default to maintenance patches unless the developer asks to upgrade
or migrate. PostgreSQL 16 → 16.15 is maintenance; 16 → 18 is a migration. Semver 5.7.3 → 5.7.4 is
a patch; 5.7 → 5.8 and 5 → 7 need upgrade scope. For 0.x packages preserve the minor as well.
Unsupported lines and fixes available only in a newer line are explicit upgrade recommendations,
not silent migrations and not reasons to stop unrelated authorized work. If no fixed patch exists
on the retained line, say so; don't claim its vulnerability is fixed. An explicit migration request
can change the selected lines and includes the necessary compatibility/data/recovery work.

Exact versions go in package manifests and locks, runtime version files and deployment definitions.
Pin production images by digest after resolving the chosen tag for the target architecture. Record
base OS, image digest, actual database server version, enabled extension versions, migration owner,
object-store implementation, browser binaries, copied component source provenance and model/index
identities. A registry tag is not a digest and a local development version is not a deployed version.
Do not invent unknown identities. Distribution security backports retain the vendor package identity.

Use `node .mock2/bin/stack.mjs init --new` for the selected new-project inventory, or
`node .mock2/bin/stack.mjs init --existing` to capture resolved npm dependencies from a lockfile
without changing any dependency. Existing non-npm stacks record their actual versions in the same
inventory manually. Initialization refuses to overwrite an existing inventory. `stack.mjs` reports
observed lockfile drift and policy; it never installs, upgrades or changes the project's toolchain.
`stack.mjs catalog` prints the selected baseline. Add this read-only report to the existing dependency
review/check workflow where useful; do not put a new gate in front of builds or releases.

Validate a dependency update as a combination, including generated schema/migrations, route and
schema behavior, types, production build, affected browser tests and deployment/runtime images.
Update React/React DOM/types together; keep Node types on the chosen runtime line. TypeScript 7
uses the native compiler and does not supply the older programmatic compiler API: tools requiring
that API need an explicit compatible bridge/version, tested separately. Pair Playwright with its
own browser binaries. Tailwind 4 requires the documented modern browser baseline. A shadcn CLI pin
alone does not pin copied UI components: record their registry/source and content hashes.

The existing Relay reference adapter retains React 18 / Express 4 / Zod 3. Its tested package pin

Every baseline review records source URLs, checked date, selected lines, support deadlines where
published, compatibility evidence and unresolved limits. Existing project patches update their
inventory/lock/image identities and affected evidence; installing newer standards does not migrate

- `relay-reference-1.2.1`: **retained-contract**. React 18 / Express 4 / Zod 3 reference adapter; new application major lines need a tested host adapter/port

# AI, retrieval and object data

These requirements extend the existing host AI, jobs, secrets, usage, permissions, storage and
realtime contracts when the corresponding capability is used. They prepare new CPR applications
for AI without adding unused services to an established application. Features consume host
capabilities; provider credentials stay sealed in host services. Keep offline fakes, scoped usage
metering and configurable provider/model selection already required by CPR.

## Embedding identity and migrations

Define an immutable embedding configuration: provider, exact model/revision, dimensions, distance
metric, normalization, input limits, extraction/chunking version and index version. Persist it with
each vector or its unambiguous index namespace. Query vectors must use the same configuration as
the index. Equal dimensions do not make different models compatible. Never silently mix spaces.

This narrows Addendum A.2's automatic sunset/failover rule: embedding-model replacement is an
explicit re-embedding migration, even when its provider calls it an alias update. Create a new index,
re-extract/re-embed as needed, evaluate retrieval and tenant/document access, switch the active
configuration, and retain the former index for the documented rollback/retention period. Failover
is allowed only to an independently verified identical space; otherwise queue/retry or report
unavailability. Do not silently query an old index using a new embedding model.

## PostgreSQL and vector retrieval

New applications start with the selected PostgreSQL 18 maintenance release and explicit pgvector
pin when vector retrieval is used. pgvector is an extension, not bundled merely by choosing a
PostgreSQL major; PostgreSQL 16 can also run it. Provision its server binaries and enable `vector`
in each authorized database through the migration owner. Check actual `server_version` and
`pg_extension.extversion` at startup/readiness and in deployment evidence. Test generated Drizzle
migrations and vector operators against the real supported server/extension pair. Extension upgrade,
restore availability, index rebuild requirements and rollback compatibility belong in the release
record. A PGlite-only test cannot establish this production contract.

Choose exact search or HNSW using measured recall/latency and memory. Verify index dimension/type
limits before picking an embedding model (pgvector HNSW vector: 2,000 dimensions; halfvec: 4,000).
Use host search APIs so storage engines can change without changing features. Combine PostgreSQL
full-text and vector candidates when lexical and semantic retrieval are both needed; reranking is
optional and evaluated. Apply tenant/document permissions in retrieval before any content enters
the model context, and test denied documents and tenants. Retrieved text is untrusted evidence;
it cannot grant permissions, execute tools or override application instructions.

## Sources, files and ingestion

Private S3-compatible object storage holds original PDFs, images, audio/video and large artifacts.
PostgreSQL holds ownership, object key/version, content hash, size/type, revision, lifecycle state,
document/chunk IDs, extraction/chunking provenance, ACLs and embedding/index state. Small structured
values or deliberately bounded blobs can stay in the database when justified; do not default large
file bytes to PostgreSQL. Choose the actual object provider under the host's existing storage
contract and record its version/identity, limits, retention and backup policy. S3 is an API contract,
not a universally versioned server product.

Use unique immutable object keys and bounded authorized uploads/downloads or short-lived signed
URLs. Validate type, size and content; scan/sandbox extraction through existing host jobs as needed.
An object write and database transaction are not atomic together: model pending/available/deleting
states with an outbox or equivalent reliable job and a reconciler for orphan/missing objects.
Never advertise an object as available before the durable write is verified. Deletion removes
sources, chunks, vectors and objects under the same host policy; backup recovery rechecks integrity.

Use the host job queue for extraction, chunking, embedding and indexing, with source-revision and
configuration-based idempotency, bounded retries/concurrency, backpressure and restart recovery.
Changed sources invalidate their prior chunks/vectors; stale jobs cannot publish over a newer
revision. Record ingestion lag, failed jobs, token/request usage and cost, and retrieval latency,
quality and access-test evidence. Do not invent provider pricing or a model-generated dollar value.

## Scale and replacement path

Start with application PostgreSQL + pgvector; isolate vector work in a dedicated PostgreSQL
deployment when measurements show contention with transactional traffic. Move to a distributed
vector engine such as the selected Qdrant release behind the same host search API when sharding,
replication, availability or measured resource limits justify it. Do not choose by a universal
vector-count threshold: dimensions, tenant filters, write/query concurrency, indexing overhead,
recall and target latency matter. One million 1,536-dimension float32 vectors alone use about
6.1 GB, before indexes, metadata and replicas.

Benchmark representative data and permissions, establish an agreed latency/quality/resource
budget, and retain source chunks and embedding configuration so an index is rebuildable. Migrate
with versioned namespaces and shadow evaluation, verify ACL/filter equivalence and deletions, then
switch the host search adapter with a tested fallback. Qdrant is a scale option, not an automatic
second database dependency for every application.

Official contracts: https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector,
https://orm.drizzle.team/docs/extensions, https://qdrant.tech/documentation/scaling/distributed_deployment/,
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/Welcome.html.

# Relay events, delivery and coding sessions

Relay's durable source is structured append-only events. A producer writes them into
`state/relay/events/`, then the authenticated host commits them with its own sequence. Relay reads
that host stream through its history API and realtime connection. Markdown ledgers, handoffs and
Git are supporting sources; changing one does not automatically create live run events. Existing
history import can extract only facts those sources actually contain.

| Event | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `task.created` / `task.updated` | Work identity and context/checkpoint/next/needs-input; no running timer |
| `run.started` | A real execution attempt began, with a unique run ID and known revision |
| `step.started` | A measured step began; dependencies describe actual ordering/parallel work |
| `step.activity` | Observed finding, heartbeat or measured progress; a heartbeat proves recent process activity, not percentage complete |
| `step.finished` | Actual passed/failed/cancelled/missing outcome, duration and revision when known |
| `run.finished` | The execution attempt ended; older failed attempts remain visible |
| `deployment.recorded` | Independently verified delivery of the named revision; a commit or successful process exit is insufficient |
| `history.commit.observed` | Repository/full-SHA/source dates observed from Git; blue history, no guessed work time or deployment |
| `check.recorded` | Executed/reused/not-run verification evidence and actual measured costs |

A start without a finish leaves an unfinished attempt. It does **not** prove that a process is
still alive: a missing/expired heartbeat is stale/unknown. Source timestamps describe chronology;
host sequence describes durable delivery/reconnect order. Duplicate event IDs are idempotent only
when content agrees; conflicting content is rejected. Local and host sequence numbers differ.

## Connect once, then deliver automatically

Use the application's existing producer identity with an explicit destination-workspace recording
grant. Supply its scoped token through the host's secret mechanism as `RELAY_INGEST_TOKEN`; supply
the credential-free HTTPS event endpoint as `RELAY_INGEST_URL`. Never put credentials in Git,
browser storage, URL query strings or pasted scripts. Set `MOCK2_WORKSPACE_ID` to the exact host
workspace. Existing human viewer access is not a producer grant.

`relay.mjs emit` and the check runner now attempt delivery automatically when configured. For
continuous delivery of events written by other producers, run `node .mock2/bin/relay.mjs watch`
under the existing host job/service or development session. This reads only structured events;
it does not scrape arbitrary files or transcripts. A bounded polling loop drains the durable outbox,
retries outages and advances its cursor only after a matching host acknowledgment. Repeated delivery
is safe. A failed delivery does not change the check/command result. Events stay local; report the
pending gap with `node .mock2/bin/relay.mjs producer-status` and retry `relay.mjs sync`.
Automatic attempts handle at most 25 events with a five-second network budget; the watcher
continues subsequent batches. Manual sync drains the retained outbox. This keeps a feed outage
from imposing unbounded delay on an otherwise completed check or command.

Record command sessions without manually constructing start/finish JSON:

```sh
node .mock2/bin/relay.mjs run --title "Implement the requested change" -- codex
```

This wraps a real foreground command, emits task/run/step boundaries and heartbeats, passes workspace,
task and run IDs to child checks, delivers during execution and on exit, and preserves its exit code.
The title is deliberately supplied context; arguments, environment and command output are not copied.
Process exit means the command ended, not that the feature was accepted or deployed. A hard kill or
machine crash may leave a stale run; do not fabricate a successful finish. The watcher and wrapper
use the existing host runtime; no separate identity/backend/database/control daemon is introduced.

## All future chats

Every coding entry point needs a producer: CLI launcher, VS Code extension/session lifecycle,
server agent harness and deployment/CI hooks. For CLI, launch each foreground coding session through
the wrapper. For an already-running VS Code agent, connect its supported lifecycle adapter or have
it emit boundaries/checkpoints through the repository rule; wrapping the VS Code application only
measures that application process, not each individual chat. A tool without accessible session hooks
cannot honestly be described as guaranteed automatic chat capture. ChatGPT conversations outside
the connected coding runtime are not discoverable by Relay's file watcher.

Use a stable task identity for continuing work and a unique run per attempt/chat, actual start/end
times, periodic heartbeats, meaningful findings and verified deployment hooks. Full transcripts are
not required for work visibility and are not copied by default. Transcript capture is a separate
authorized retention/audience capability. The install acceptance test must start a **new** session,
observe its local events, verify host acknowledgment and read it back in the same workspace, then
finish it and verify its terminal state. Also test outage/restart, duplicate delivery and revoked
producer scope. A page saying Connected verifies the viewer transport only.

## Historical commits and established hosts

Relay 1.2-compatible hosts can connect an authorized backend checkout/repository ID and destination
workspace using `relay.mjs init`, then perform the resumable initial Git lookback described in
`Relay.md`. Preserve full commit SHAs, parent SHAs and original source dates. Link native run/deployment
records using their actual revision; commit observations themselves never imply those outcomes.
Production files need not contain `.git`: use the development/source checkout or the host's
authorized repository-provider adapter.

If an established host already has a review-first importer, preserve that mode. Use its Import
history preview, select the repository Git source and import the reviewed records. A host still on
Relay 1.1.x rejects the new version-2 commit/check vocabulary: migrate its readers/storage/UI through
its normal release process before enabling 1.2 producers. Merely installing newer standards does
not upgrade a host-native adapter. Do not silently filter rejected event types or mark them delivered.

Record three independent results in the app handoff: viewer installed, ongoing producer delivery
verified, worker control acknowledgments verified. For historical import, additionally record source
repository, window/cursor, shallow status, destination workspace and actual import/delivery result.
Missing connectivity or unsupported hooks remain visible, not replaced with simulated activity.

# Universal integration foundation

Introduced in Mock2 1.14.0. This is a framework- and vendor-neutral standard;
healthcare examples in the companion prompts are illustrative, not required domain models.

## Choose the implementation path

- **New application:** follow `Universal-Integration-New-App-Prompt.md`. Establish the small
  working foundation during the initial build, even with no external connections. Define only
  relevant domain contracts; do not invent vendors or install speculative infrastructure.
- **Existing application:** when integration modernization is requested, follow
  `Universal-Integration-Existing-App-Prompt.md`. Inventory, wrap working services, add compatible
  mappings, and migrate actual callers in verified vertical slices. Finish all identified
  in-scope features, or explicitly name deferred features and their functioning old paths.
- **Standards-only upgrade or unrelated maintenance:** distribute these instructions and record
  applicability; do not silently migrate application code, schemas, dependencies or connections.

Both companion prompts are complete implementation instructions. This document defines the shared
boundaries and acceptance evidence. User scope and existing approved application decisions govern.

## Logical architecture

Use modules in the current application and its existing persistence, permissions, secrets, jobs,
audit and release mechanisms. CPR-profile features consume those capabilities through their Host
Contract/SDK. Other profiles reuse their own equivalents. No new identity provider, microservices,
visual workflow designer, ORM or orchestration engine is implied.

| Boundary | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| Domain identity and external mappings | Stable internal references and authorized, recoverable links to scoped source records |
| Connection registry | Specific tenant-owned instance/account/organization, provider, environment, namespaces, credential references, configuration, lifecycle and health |
| Versioned feature contracts | Required outcomes and semantics independent of vendor implementation |
| Adapters and workflows | Vendor calls, transformations and bounded call sequences implementing a contract |
| Capability registry | Evidence of semantic support per connection and contract version |
| Authorized dispatcher | Actor/scope checks, mapping resolution, compatible implementation selection, execution and result validation |

External mapping keys include **tenant, connection, source namespace/organization, resource type
and external ID**. IDs are scoped strings. Preserve source identifiers and provenance. Keep login
accounts distinct from domain people and records where appropriate; a representative is not
necessarily the subject. A person ID alone neither chooses a source nor grants access. Linking,
merging and unlinking require authorization, audit and recovery; never merge automatically from
name, birth date or email. Report ambiguous links and missing namespaces rather than guessing.
Disconnection prevents execution while retaining mappings and history. Secrets remain references
to existing secure storage, never values in these records or documentation.

## Contract and execution semantics

Each contract defines inputs and internal references; tenant/actor/connection scope; permission
requirements; preconditions and side effects; success and required/optional fields; filtering,
pagination and ordering; time-zone/status semantics; freshness, provenance and completeness;
normalized errors and explicit partial-result policy; version compatibility. Breaking semantic
changes require explicit version handling. An adapter must not silently weaken the outcome or
invent missing values. Domain schemas remain separate from the reusable core.

An adapter can make one call or several. Compose public features only for independently meaningful
outcomes; otherwise use private helpers. For example, a roster can compose `appointments.list`
with `person.summary.get`, without fetching full demographics on every appointment query.
Propagate authorized source scope, prevent cycles, bound time/calls, and batch/cache with tenant
and permission isolation. Use durable host jobs only where asynchronous waits or recovery need them.

Capabilities are **verified full**, **partial**, **unsupported**, or **unverified**, per connection
and contract version. Record limitations, required permissions, evidence, verification date and
implementation version. Keep enabled/configured state, health and current authorization separate.
A vendor name, endpoint or discovery metadata is not proof of contract compliance. Partial support
is usable only where the contract and caller permit it; revalidate evidence after relevant changes.

Dispatch checks app and applicable source permissions, resolves identities within the requested
scope, selects a compatible implementation, executes and validates normalized results. Broad service
credentials must not broaden a user's access. Multiple sources require an explicit connection or
authorized aggregation policy. Define what “all” means: source set, date/filter boundaries,
pagination and completion. Expose per-source failures and overall completeness. An inaccessible or
failed source is not an empty success. Deduplicate only with established evidence.

Apply bounded timeouts, rate-limit handling, safe retries and write idempotency. An uncertain write
must not be blindly retried. Multi-system writes require explicit recovery or compensation; there
is no implied distributed transaction. Trace correlation IDs, source, contract/implementation
versions, timing and sanitized outcomes through existing audit/Relay when available, excluding
credentials and sensitive payloads.

## Implementation and migration evidence

For a new app, provide identity-map interfaces, connection and capability registries, relevant
contract definitions, adapter interface and dispatcher, with persistence where appropriate. Empty
connections are valid: local features keep working and external features return not-configured.
App-owned implementations may satisfy relevant contracts. Mocks stay in development/tests.
Scaffolding, fake conformance and live vendor verification are reported separately.

For an existing app, trace UI/API/jobs through current vendor behavior and first produce the
crosswalk below. Reuse sound internal IDs; where source IDs serve as local identity, add compatible
internal identity and preserve references/URLs. Backfills are additive, resumable and idempotent;
report collisions, ambiguity, unmatched records and missing source context. Never assign an
ambiguous record to a default organization.

Wrap current integration services before replacing internals. Preserve credentials, consent,
checkpoints, source configuration, permissions and event history. Do not disconnect/reconnect as a
migration shortcut. Reauthentication requires an actual credential/consent/scope/vendor dependency;
state the smallest necessary change. Start with one low-risk read and an actual caller, then its
compositions, other reads and separately controlled writes. Compare old/new identifiers, counts,
filters, pagination, authorization, errors and completeness using fixtures or approved read-only
shadow execution, accounting for changing source data. Never shadow-execute production writes.

Use the existing staged release mechanism and preserve compatible old paths until verified.
Fallback cannot bypass permissions or capability restrictions. Rollback preserves new mappings
and writes; destructive schema rollback is not a recovery plan. Retire old paths only after
replacement evidence is sufficient. Keep the app usable with no external connection.

Maintain `state/integrations.md` or the app's established equivalent, with:

- Current feature/caller, identifiers, connection/source scope, observed outcome, proposed contract,
  existing implementation to wrap, limitations, migration risk and validation method.
- Actual modules/data model, contract catalog, per-connection capability matrix and evidence.
- Backfill/collision results, migrated and unmigrated callers, cutover/rollback and reconnection needs.
- How to add a second adapter or compose a feature, plus explicit remaining limitations.

Acceptance uses meaningful app-stack tests for namespaced collisions, tenant/permission isolation,
mapping ambiguity, multiple connections and routing, result validation, composition, partial support,
pagination, source failures, empty connections, and applicable retry/write safety. Supply reusable
adapter-conformance checks. Existing-app evidence additionally covers preserved references and
old/new comparisons. These are application acceptance obligations, not claims that installing
this standards release has implemented or verified an application's integration.

## Adoption

The normal Mock2 installer and repository upgrade distribute this standard, both prompts, the
managed entry pointers and a project-owned record template. The upgrade preserves edited files
and existing project records under the established ownership policy. For existing repositories,
read the applicable canonical instructions even if their project-owned checklist was preserved.
No application migration or new external account is a side effect of updating the standards.

Implement a universal integration foundation for this new application.

GOAL
Build the app so its features depend on stable internal identities and versioned feature contracts. Each connected system implements those contracts through its own adapter or workflow. A feature describes the required outcome; its implementation may use one API call, several calls, or other features.

The foundation must work before any external system is connected. Keep it framework and vendor agnostic, with domain-specific modules where needed. Healthcare examples below are illustrative; do not add patient or appointment models to unrelated apps.

1. Inspect and fit the application
Read repository instructions, applicable Mock2/CPR standards, existing architecture, authentication, permissions, persistence, testing, and release process. Reuse those systems and approved dependencies. Verify current official documentation for any vendor integration you actually implement. Do the implementation and appropriate verification; do not stop at a proposal.

Start with modules in the existing application. Do not introduce microservices, a visual workflow designer, a new identity provider, or a separate workflow engine merely to create this foundation.

2. Separate internal identity from external records and login accounts
Give relevant entities stable internal identifiers. Keep a person, a patient/customer record, a contact/representative, an employee/provider record, and a login account distinct. Use explicit relationships where appropriate.

Map external records to internal entities using a key that includes tenant, connection, source namespace/organization, resource type, and external ID. Treat external IDs as scoped strings, never globally unique identifiers. One person may have records in multiple practices or systems. A contact is not necessarily the subject of the record.

Record link provenance, verification state, and timestamps. Linking, merging, or unlinking identity records must be authorized, audited, and recoverable. Similar names, dates of birth, or email addresses may suggest candidates; they must not automatically establish identity. Do not make identity linkage grant access or cross tenant boundaries.

3. Define a registry of connections
Each connection represents a specific authorized instance, practice, account, or organization, not just a vendor name. Include tenant/organization ownership, provider type, external namespaces, environment, credential references, configuration, lifecycle state, and health. Keep secrets in existing secure storage.

Support multiple connections to the same vendor and different capabilities per connection. Disconnection must preserve identity mappings and history while preventing execution through that connection.

4. Create versioned feature contracts
Define contracts for the app's actual integration-related outcomes. Examples are appointments.list, person.summary.get, or contacts.list. Separate the reusable core from domain schemas; avoid a single universal object with every vendor's fields.

Each contract must specify:
- Meaning of success and the required result fields.
- Inputs, entity references, tenant/connection scope, and authorization requirements.
- Preconditions, side effects, validation, and applicable time-zone/status semantics.
- Pagination, date/filter boundaries, ordering guarantees, freshness, and completeness.
- Errors, permitted partial results, and behavior when required data is unavailable.
- Version and compatibility rules; breaking semantic changes require explicit version handling.

Preserve source identifiers and provenance. Optional fields may be absent with a documented reason. Do not invent missing values or silently substitute a weaker outcome.

5. Implement adapters, workflows, and feature composition
Keep vendor URLs, payloads, credentials, and call sequences inside integration modules. Each implementation maps source behavior into the declared contract.

One system might need two requests for a person summary and another only one. That difference belongs in their implementations. Features may compose other features when those outcomes are independently meaningful; private API helpers need not become public features.

An appointments list can return identifiers, times, statuses, and source context. A roster requiring names can compose appointments.list with person.summary.get. Do not fetch full demographics for every appointment query by default.

Preserve the authorized connection scope across dependent calls. Prevent dependency cycles, bound calls/time, and batch or cache appropriately without leaking data across tenants. Use ordinary application services for simple workflows; durable orchestration is justified only by long-running, asynchronous, or recoverable work.

6. Track capabilities honestly
Maintain capability records per connection and feature contract version. Distinguish verified full support, partial support, unsupported, and unverified. Track configuration, current authorization, and connection health separately from semantic support.

Record limitations, required permissions, evidence, verification date, and implementation version. Vendor discovery metadata is evidence, not proof that a workflow meets the contract. Partial support is usable only where the contract and caller explicitly allow that result.

7. Route and execute safely
The app calls a feature with explicit tenant, actor, scope, and internal references. The runtime checks permission, resolves mappings, selects compatible implementations for the requested connections, executes, validates, and returns normalized results.

Do not choose a source solely from a person ID. If multiple sources are possible, require an explicit connection or an authorized aggregation policy.

For 'all appointments,' define authorized connections, date range, filters, pagination, and a completion policy. Report source-specific failures and overall completeness; a failed source must not look like an empty successful result. Deduplicate only using established identity/event evidence.

Enforce access through the app and the applicable source permissions. Broad integration credentials must not broaden employee access. Add appropriate timeouts, rate-limit handling, safe retries, and write idempotency. Do not retry an uncertain write blindly. Multi-system writes need explicit recovery/compensation; do not imply a shared transaction.

8. Make the foundation usable without integrations
Provide the identity-map interfaces, connection registry, contract definitions, adapter interface, capability registry, dispatcher, and documentation. Persist configuration and mappings where appropriate using the existing datastore. Keep local features working through existing application services; an app-owned implementation may satisfy relevant contracts.

An empty connection registry is valid. External features return a clear not-configured result when no source exists. Keep mock data explicitly confined to development/tests. Do not require a vendor account or build speculative integrations.

9. Verify and deliver
Use meaningful tests for namespaced identity collisions, tenant/permission isolation, per-connection routing, contract validation, composition, missing mappings, partial support, pagination, empty connections, and applicable write safety. Include conformance checks reusable by future adapters.

Document the actual modules/data model, initial contract catalog, capability matrix, execution flow, and how to add an adapter or compose a feature. Trace executions with source, contract/implementation versions, correlation ID, timing, and sanitized outcomes. Reuse existing audit/Relay observability if present; keep credentials and sensitive payloads out of routine logs.

Report implemented functionality, validation evidence, limitations, and remaining integrations. Distinguish verified implementations from scaffolding. The result should be a small working foundation that future connections extend without forcing a redesign of application features.

Incrementally adapt this existing application to a universal integration foundation.

GOAL

Complete the authorized implementation and verification; do not stop at an architecture proposal.

Use a gradual migration: inventory the current behavior, wrap existing integration code, add compatible identity mappings, move one feature at a time, and retire old paths only after their replacements are verified.

7. Migrate a vertical slice and expand
Choose a low-risk read feature, such as listing appointments or contacts, as the first complete slice. Map it, wrap its current implementation, route an actual caller through the contract, and verify results. Then migrate its required compositions, other reads, and separately controlled writes.

Compare old/new read results using fixtures, captured test data, or approved read-only shadow execution. Control for changes in source data and verify identifiers, counts, filters, pagination, permissions, errors, and completeness. Never shadow-execute or duplicate production writes.

Use the existing release/feature-flag mechanism for staged cutover. Maintain a compatible old path until validation passes. Rollback must preserve new identity mappings and writes; do not make a destructive schema rollback the recovery strategy. Fallback must preserve authorization and must not bypass capability restrictions.

After a successful slice, continue through the identified in-scope features in dependency order. Mark any deferred feature explicitly and keep its current functioning route. An app with no external connections must remain usable.

8. Verify, document, and finish
Run appropriate regression and adapter-conformance checks. Cover tenant isolation, identity collisions, preserved references, mapping ambiguity, multiple connections, contract semantics, composition, partial capabilities, pagination, disconnected sources, and applicable write/retry safety.

Document the implemented architecture, migration/crosswalk table, data/backfill results, contract catalog, per-connection capability matrix, cutover/rollback procedure, and how a second vendor adapter can be added. Reuse existing audit/Relay tracing when present, with correlation IDs and contract/source/version evidence. Keep credentials and sensitive payloads out of routine logs.

Report exactly which callers/features now use the foundation, which still use existing paths, what was tested, any required reconnection, unresolved mapping issues, and remaining limitations. Follow the project's authorized review and release process. Do not claim completion for unverified adapters or silently abandon unmigrated in-scope behavior.
