# Mock2 capacity, delivery and handoff

Standards version: <stamped from ~/.mock2/version at scaffold time>

How work is sized against what one agent turn can do, what a turn owes before it returns, and how a
turn ends so the next one starts cheaply.

None of this is a gate (constitution rule 0). It never refuses, delays or narrows what the developer
asked for. The duties here fall on the agent.

## 1. Runs, turns, items, authorized scope

- A **run** is one bounded, verifiable work package. If a turn ends before its stopping condition is
  met, later turns continue the same run. A run is defined by acceptance scope, never by how many
  responses it took.
- A **turn** is one complete agent execution between a user message and the agent's final response —
  not each intermediate progress message.
- An **item** is one row in `state/work.md`, sized (§4) and decomposed until independently executable
  and verifiable.
- The **currently authorized task** is the scope established by the user's instructions. The run plan
  records and decomposes that scope; it cannot expand authorization. Continue through all plan items
  within that scope unless the user redirects the task or a supported stopping reason applies. The
  scope is written down once, before the first code change, as the Authorized scope record (§13).

Reported as:

```
Run: 3 of 6
Turn within run: 2
Run status: IN PROGRESS
Outcome produced: yes | no
Turn result: AUTHORIZED TASK COMPLETE | STOPPING CONDITION MET | BUDGET STOP | STOPPED SHORT | HANDED OFF | BLOCKED | CANCELLED | SCOPE CHANGED
```

Outcome and turn result are independent. A turn can produce an outcome and still have stopped short.

**Run boundaries are checkpoints, not stops.** When a run's stopping condition passes, its checks are
green, and the next run does not depend on a question still undecided, continue into the next run in
the same turn.

## 2. When to classify

Classify before implementing when there is no valid run plan covering the request, and any of:

- the request names more than one acceptance item, numbered requirement or checklist section;
- the derived work file contains an L or XL item, or exceeds a run's budget (§4);
- the request says finish, complete, all of, everything, or names a whole workflow.

**A valid existing plan takes precedence over reclassification.** If `state/work.md` holds a plan
covering the request, resume it (§11). Classify again only when no plan exists, or the plan does not
cover what was asked. A plan never authorizes work the user did not ask for; where a plan item falls
outside the current instruction, say so rather than implementing it.

Do not classify — start implementing — when the change is size-router trivial (typo, config tweak,
obvious bug, behavior unchanged), or the work is within one run's budget and names a single
acceptance item.

## 3. What classification may read

`state/work.md`, `state/rules.md`, `state/decisions.md`, `state/handoff.md`,
`state/production-checklist.md`, `000-READ-FIRST.md`, and the developer's request.

Targeted inspection of a named file is allowed when the state files are insufficient to size an item
— read it, say why. What is prohibited is the repeated broad audit: sweeping the tree, re-deriving
architecture, re-running discovery already recorded in `000-READ-FIRST.md`.

If sizing still cannot be settled, return SPLIT with RUN 1 = "establish the facts needed to size the
rest", naming exactly what will be read. That run is a **bounded investigation**: its assigned purpose
is findings, and it completes on concrete recorded findings (§6). It may never be substituted for an
implementation task that is already actionable.

Whole classification output: at most 25 lines.

## 4. Sizing and decomposition

Sizes are planning estimates from the acceptance language and prior run history. They are not
capability guarantees; an estimate proven wrong is corrected (§12), not defended.

| Size | Points | Meaning |
|---|---:|---|
| S | 1 | Localized change with one directly exercising check. |
| M | 2 | Several related files, or one layer boundary, with focused tests. |
| L | 4 | Cross-layer behavior, a migration, an accessibility surface, a new execution path, or work needing browser verification. |
| XL | — | Architectural replacement, a workflow end to end, replacing an engine or evaluator. Never scheduled; decomposed first. |

**A run's budget is 4 points.** Only leaf items are scheduled and consume budget; a decomposed parent
is a container.

**Decomposition stops when an item is independently executable and verifiable** — not when its size
label falls below L. A leaf may be L: browser verification at three viewports is one executable,
verifiable unit and consumes a whole run. Only XL is barred from scheduling.

```
W7    Accessible source navigator                             L    (container, not scheduled)
W7.1  Replace native relation picker with controlled tree     M
W7.2  Hierarchical ARIA and roving focus                      M
W7.3  Buffered typeahead                                      S
W7.4  Request cancellation and stale-response protection      M
W7.5  Source Setup tree component coverage                    M
W7.6  Responsive bottom-sheet behavior                        S
W7.7  320 px, desktop and 200% browser coverage               L    (leaf — one run)
```

## 5. The three verdicts

**FITS** — within one run's budget. State the points. Start.

```
CAPACITY: FITS — W1 S, W2 S, W3 M = 4 points, one run.
```

**SPLIT** — emit a run plan, write it into `state/work.md`, start RUN 1 and continue through run
boundaries per §1.

```
CAPACITY: SPLIT — 11 acceptance items → 6 runs.
RUN 1  Setup-owned bucket rule lifecycle          W1.1 M, W1.2 M   4 pts
       stop: W1.1-W1.2 VERIFIED — catch-all-last enforced and stale-revision rejected, shown by
             `npm run check:test -- server/buckets`; work.md updated; staged diff reviewed
RUN 2  ...
COVERAGE: 11 of 11 acceptance items placed, none duplicated, no XL scheduled.
```

Each entry states number, objective, leaf item IDs with sizes, point total, and a stopping condition
that names the acceptance behavior demonstrated and the commands or files that demonstrate it — not
merely commands that exit zero. A stopping condition written only in prose is not one. `COVERAGE:` is
required.

**CANNOT** — a named part is outside what this agent can do here. Give the part and its class: missing
credential or access; a tool not present; a decision only the developer can make; an unbounded
unknown; a physical limit. Then deliver the largest reachable subset and record the remainder as an
Open item. CANNOT is a report, never a refusal.

## 6. What a turn owes before it returns

A turn working a run produces at least one **recorded verifiable outcome**, in one of three shapes.

**Implementation outcome** — make the source or test change, run the check that directly exercises it,
repair what the change broke, record the result. Re-running a check to confirm a repair, or to
establish whether a failure is flaky, is part of this and is expected.

**Validation outcome** — running a named check counts when it *completes a pending verification
requirement* or *establishes materially new evidence needed for the next action*. Re-running an
unchanged known failure is not new progress. Recording an in-scope failure creates a repair
obligation: it does not authorize ending the turn while that repair is actionable.

**Bounded-investigation outcome** — a run whose assigned purpose is establishing facts (§3) completes
on concrete recorded findings. It never substitutes for an implementation task already actionable.

Searches, file reads, plans and described edits are not outcomes. When the exact file, symbol and
required behavior have been identified on an implementation run, the edit is made in that turn;
returning with it described is not permitted. An unnecessary edit is not an outcome either — code that
is already correct is validated, not touched.

**Validation provenance.** Follow `.mock2/standards/rules/mock2-verification.md`. Record command,
result/skips, original execution time/run, complete input/tool/configuration/environment identity,
and any later invalidation. Label valid earlier evidence **reused — inputs unchanged** when those
inputs and freshness conditions are proven to match. Label invalidated or unproven evidence
**historical**. Do not imply reuse ran again. Revalidate affected inputs after edits or rebases;
broad or uncertain impact requires the full applicable set. Keep one canonical run record and link
or generate repeated facts in the handoff and change record; preserve authored decisions and history.

A turn returning having produced none of the three shapes, without a supported stopping reason (§7),
is `STOPPED SHORT`.

This is a duty on the agent, not a restriction on the developer, and never a reason to delay or refuse
requested work (rule 0).

## 7. How a turn ends

```
Turn id: <YYYY-MM-DD>-<n>
Outcome produced: yes | no — <which shape, and what>
Turn result: <one of the below>
Tool calls this turn: <n> | unknown
Continue prompt seen: yes | no | unknown
```

- **AUTHORIZED TASK COMPLETE** — the scope the user established is finished. The normal successful end
  of a response.
- **STOPPING CONDITION MET** — a run's stopping condition passed. **A checkpoint, not permission to
  end.** Use it as the turn result only where the user scoped the turn to that run; otherwise continue
  (§1).
- **BUDGET STOP** — an actual limit required stopping, quoted verbatim: a hard context or tool-call
  ceiling, an iteration ceiling, or a budget the developer set.
- **STOPPED SHORT** — returned while the authorized task was incomplete and work on it was actionable,
  with no supported stopping reason. Applies **whether or not an outcome was produced**: one small edit
  followed by an unexplained return is STOPPED SHORT.
- **HANDED OFF** — everything this surface can do on the authorized task is done and verified as
  far as this surface can verify it, and the remainder needs a capability this surface lacks by
  design (push, deploy, database, provider access). The evidence is the line in `## Surfaces` in
  `.github/copilot-instructions.md` that shows the missing capability (CPR §M.2). The first turn that
  needs the section adds it; a line an agent adds is marked `(unconfirmed)` until the developer keeps
  it, and a HANDED OFF turn citing an unconfirmed line also quotes the failure the surface actually
  hit (the push error, the absent client). The handoff carries a *Finish on another surface* section naming the
  surface and the exact next action. It is not a failure and not a block. It is never used while
  work this surface can do remains.
- **BLOCKED** — an unplanned, externally evidenced impossibility, evidence quoted. A capability the
  surface was never meant to have is HANDED OFF, not BLOCKED.
- **CANCELLED** — the developer interrupted, including "stop and save" and "pause". On "stop and
  save", start nothing new, commit what is verified on the session's branch, record the exact next
  step and say what is left. On "pause", stop background work too, write nothing more, and report
  what was written where; its ledger row and handoff entry are written on resume (CPR §M.7).
  **SCOPE CHANGED** — the developer redirected. Neither counts toward §9.

`ENVIRONMENT BOUNDARY` is deliberately absent. A hard boundary normally ends the turn before anything
can be written, so a record claiming one is usually something else. A later turn can observe only that
the handoff is stale — never why (§8).

Where the surface reports nothing about tool calls or continue prompts, record `unknown`. Do not infer
a platform limit from a short turn.

**Reported context consumption prepares state; it does not by itself end the task.** At 60%, avoid
starting an L leaf item; at 75%, bring the current leaf item to a verifiable state and refresh the
handoff; at 85%, keep durable state current after every item. Checkpoint guidance, not stopping rules.
A compaction or summarization notice is a reason to make state durable, not a reason to stop — where
the environment continues through compaction, continue. Stop when an actual limit requires it or the
developer set that boundary. Where nothing is reported, do not guess or announce a number.

## 8. Accounting for the previous turn

Before work, a turn resuming an OPEN plan reads `state/handoff.md` and the Run history in
`state/work.md`, then:

1. If the previous turn already has a row in the Run history, that prevents **duplication, not
   review**. Validate the row against the handoff's evidence — was an outcome actually produced, was
   any validation executed, validly reused or historical, was the result honestly labelled — and correct it where wrong.
2. Where no row exists, add one from the handoff, corrected the same way.
3. Record whatever concrete progress the turn made, even where the item remains unverified.
4. **Derive** the count, never trusting a stored number: walk the Run history backwards from the most
   recent row, skipping rows marked CANCELLED, SCOPE CHANGED, BLOCKED or BUDGET STOP with quoted
   evidence, and HANDED OFF citing a confirmed `## Surfaces` line or quoting the failure the surface
   hit — those are ineligible and transparent to the walk. A HANDED OFF row without that citation is validated like any other return. Count
   consecutive eligible rows whose corrected result is `STOPPED SHORT`, stopping at the first
   eligible row that is not.
5. At two, apply §9 before starting work.

If `state/handoff.md` is older than HEAD, or the tree holds changes the handoff does not account for,
record `handoff stale — cause unknown`. In a tree another session shares, judge this per session
section of the handoff (CPR §M.1): another session's commit does not make this section stale. Do not attribute it to an interruption: someone else may have
edited the tree, or the previous turn may have skipped its update. Inspect before assigning changes to
this run; list what cannot be attributed as unknown.

## 9. Repeated-insufficient-progress breaker

A derived count (§8) of two establishes **repeated insufficient progress** on this branch. That is
what is known; the cause is not. Record it in the Run history with the surface name and the tool-call
counts, `unknown` included. The classification clears when §8's derivation returns fewer than two.

The next turn does not reissue the same instruction. It does exactly one of:

1. **Reduce the next execution unit to one leaf item — without reducing the authorized task.** After
   verifying that item, continue to the next actionable item while execution remains available.
2. Decompose the current item into leaf sub-items and take the first, then continue as above.
3. Prepare a complete handoff for another execution surface and say so. This is for when local work
   genuinely cannot proceed — not an escape route while useful local work remains possible. Moving
   work, repositories or credentials between environments needs the developer's authorization; these
   standards do not grant it. Propose the move; do not perform it.

Record the choice and reason in `state/handoff.md`. Reissuing a broad completion instruction after two
STOPPED SHORT turns is prohibited: it spends context without changing the result. Two turns is a
deliberately small sample — a false positive costs one smaller execution unit, a false negative costs a
run.

## 10. Verification and commits

An item is **VERIFIED** when its acceptance behavior is implemented and the relevant checks demonstrate
that behavior. A command's successful exit alone does not establish acceptance coverage: a typecheck
can pass while the path it covers is still wrong, and a test can pass without exercising the required
behavior. Commit status is recorded separately and is not part of the definition.

Commit after a VERIFIED item, or at a coherent verified checkpoint. Before committing: inspect
`git status --short`; stage only the files belonging to the item; inspect the staged diff; confirm the
focused checks pass; never stage broadly while unrelated changes are in the tree.

A session that may run at the same time as another works in its own worktree (CPR §M.1). Where a tree
is shared anyway, the index holds whatever any session staged, so `git add <path> && git commit`
commits all of it. Add new files by name (`git add -- <new files>`), check
`git diff HEAD --stat -- <paths>`, commit with `git commit --only -- <paths>`, and confirm with
`git show --stat HEAD`. `--only` takes the working-tree content of each path, including another
session's edits to the same file: such a file is committed only by staging this session's hunks and
committing with no paths once `git diff --cached --stat` shows nothing else (stage hunks with
`git apply --cached <patch>` where the surface has no interactive `git add -p`). Leaving such a file
uncommitted, and saying so in the handoff, is the default. Where concurrent sessions keep the
shared records in the checkout releases run from, that checkout is not a working tree for any
session: sessions edit records there by targeted insert, and the release step commits them
(CPR §M.4).

If a turn ends mid-item, leave it IN PROGRESS and record the dirty files and failing check in the
handoff. A WIP commit is made only when one is needed to move work between environments; it never marks
an item complete.

## 11. Continuation runs

A turn resuming an OPEN plan reads `state/handoff.md`, `000-READ-FIRST.md`, `state/work.md`,
`state/decisions.md` and `state/rules.md` first, then begins at the named next subtask. It does not
re-derive the work file, re-audit the tree, or restate the plan. Targeted reads of files the handoff
names are expected; broad discovery is not.

An ACTIVE record in `state/decisions.md` outranks historical conversation (CPR §17.3), so a prior
decision is not reopened or re-offered as alternatives. **The developer's current explicit instruction
outranks both.** A live instruction never loses authority because it has not been copied into the
ledger yet — record it, superseding the stale entry, then do the dependent work. Never ask the
developer to repeat a decision they have already given.

Repository-wide orientation is paid once per branch, into `000-READ-FIRST.md`. A second broad pass on
the same branch needs a stated reason — the tree changed outside this branch's commits, or the handoff
is missing — recorded in the change record.

If `.mock2/capacity.md` is missing from a repo, apply the guidance available and say the file is
absent. Do not scaffold it as part of an implementation request: standards are installed through
mock2-setup or mock2-adopt.

## 12. Correcting a plan

When an item proves larger than its size, promote it (S→M, M→L, L→XL), decompose if it reached XL or is
not yet independently verifiable, re-cut the remaining runs from what is already known, and record the
promotion with one line of reason. **Subdividing an item within its existing acceptance scope is free
and needs no permission**, however often it proves necessary; it reads nothing new and is not a
reassessment.

What stops and asks is changing the plan's shape: adding or dropping acceptance coverage, or a
correction that would change the outcome, the authority needed, the risk, or a budget the developer
set. Say which, and ask. Within a cycle, the answer to "should this be added" is one of the three
labels in §13 — never a silent addition.

## 13. Authorized scope record and findings during work

Done is defined before the first code change, not discovered during implementation and review. The
cost of leaving it undefined is a review that finds one more condition each round.

Before the first code change of a cycle — during classification (§2), or in the same turn when the
work is not classified — write the scope once into `state/work.md` under `## Authorized scope`. Add
the section if the file predates it. It is the developer's instructions written down, at the level
they gave them; it is not a design and not a questionnaire for the developer.

```
## Authorized scope: <feature>
Outcome: <who can do what when this is done — one sentence>
Done when: <the R-### rules, or W items, whose demonstrated acceptance behavior means done>
Failure cases that count as done: <only those this change touches — interruption, retry,
  existing data, conflicting operation, wrong person — or "none">
Excluded: <what this cycle does not do>
Prerequisites found during inspection: <P-1 what — why the outcome needs it — what closes it,
  or "none">
```

A small change gets three lines. Writing it is never a reason to delay the edit: write it and continue
in the same turn. After the first code change the record is not edited except as this section allows,
and it is never rewritten afterwards to match what was built.

**Every finding during implementation or review gets exactly one label:**

- **IN SCOPE** — an ID already under Done when needs it. Fix it in this cycle; note it under that ID.
  A defect this change introduced, or one on a code path this change adds or newly calls, is IN
  SCOPE under the ID the change serves: it is part of the change, not a defect elsewhere. A defect
  that already existed and was only discovered during the work stays FOLLOW-UP.
- **PREREQUISITE** — the outcome cannot be reached without it. Add it under Prerequisites with an ID
  and the reason, fix it, and add nothing else on its account.
- **FOLLOW-UP** — everything else: a better design, a case the scope does not promise, a defect
  elsewhere, an idea. One line under `## Follow-ups` in `state/work.md`, starting with its severity;
  not done this cycle and not discussed further this turn. A finding being real does not move it out
  of this label.

The label decides what this cycle does, not whether the developer hears about it. A FOLLOW-UP that
concerns security (authorization, data visible across owners or tenants, credentials) or data
integrity (loss, corruption, a deadlock, a write that can apply twice) is marked `SECURITY` or
`DATA` on its line and is also named in the handoff and at the top of the change record's Open items,
in the turn it is found. An agent never deletes a Follow-ups line to shorten the list: lines leave
it when the developer triages them (promote to a task, accept, or drop with a word of reason) or when
the work file is cleared at the end of a cycle, after the change record has copied them into Open
items. When the list has grown past a single reading, the handoff reports its length and its marked
lines.

An ID is added mid-cycle only as PREREQUISITE. Widening Done when because a reviewer would have built
it differently, or because a case is possible rather than promised, is prohibited. Only IN SCOPE and
PREREQUISITE findings hold the cycle open; the cycle is complete when every Done-when ID is VERIFIED,
whatever the length of the Follow-ups list. The Mock2 Reviewer uses the same three labels; its
FOLLOW-UP findings go into the change record's Open items or Proposals, where the developer decides
whether any becomes a later authorized task.

The developer may widen the scope at any time; that is SCOPE CHANGED (§7), recorded in the Authorized
scope block with the date, and it is the one way Done when grows other than PREREQUISITE.

## 14. Anti-patterns

- Returning with the edit described but not attempted.
- Re-running a known unchanged failure and recording it as progress.
- Presenting earlier evidence as freshly executed, reusing it without proven matching inputs and
  freshness, or omitting the original execution time and tested state.
- Recording an in-scope failure and ending the turn while its repair is actionable.
- Calling an item VERIFIED because a command exited zero, without the acceptance behavior demonstrated.
- Ending the response because one run's stopping condition passed while authorized work remains.
- Treating the run plan as authorization for work the user did not ask for.
- Reducing the authorized task when the breaker fires, rather than the next execution unit; or
  preparing a transfer handoff while useful local work remains.
- Treating a compaction notice, or a context percentage, as a reason to stop.
- Recording `boundary` or `blocked` for a turn that chose to return; recording a planned hand-off to
  another surface as BLOCKED.
- Inferring a platform limit, or a cause for a stale handoff, from what a short turn looks like.
- Trusting a stored count instead of deriving it from history, or accepting a previous turn's
  self-reported result without validating it against its evidence.
- Reissuing the same broad instruction after two STOPPED SHORT turns.
- Running a repository-wide assessment when the plan status is OPEN, or reclassifying when a valid plan
  covers the request.
- Reopening a decision recorded ACTIVE — or refusing a current instruction because the ledger disagrees.
- Scheduling an XL item; counting a decomposed parent against a run's budget; splitting an item already
  independently executable and verifiable.
- Marking an item complete because a commit exists; committing with `git add -A` while unrelated
  changes are present; committing in a tree another session shares without an explicit path list.
- Editing code that is already correct to satisfy §6.
- Scaffolding missing standards files during an implementation request.
- Starting code without the Authorized scope written, or rewriting it afterwards to match what was
  built.
- Adding an acceptance ID mid-cycle for a finding that is not a prerequisite of the outcome; treating
  a possible case as a promised one; fixing a FOLLOW-UP because it was easy.

## 15. What this is judged by

Not by whether the bookkeeping is complete. By completed acceptance requirements, meaningful checks
demonstrating the behavior, and fewer user continuations needed to get there. If keeping
`state/work.md` and `state/handoff.md` current is displacing implementation rather than supporting it,
the bookkeeping is wrong and gets cut — duplicate factual transcription first. Use the canonical
per-run evidence to populate views, retaining original times and measured provenance. The standards'
verification rule describes a controlled before/after comparison; compare time and acceptance quality
on the same tasks, not ledger completeness.
